The peritoneum is a serous membrane that lines the abdominal cavity (parietal peritoneum) and covers the abdominal organs (visceral peritoneum).

In this autopsy image, you can see the glistening, smooth, semi-transparent layer covering the loops of the intestines; this is the **visceral peritoneum**.

While the abdominal wall has been opened to expose the organs (meaning the peritoneal cavity is now open to the air), the membrane itself remains present on the surfaces of the organs and the inner lining of the body wall.

Based on the provided image of an open abdominal cavity:

Yes, the peritoneum is present. The peritoneum is the serous membrane that lines the abdominal cavity (parietal peritoneum) and covers the abdominal organs (visceral peritoneum).

The most striking finding in this image is the extensive presence of small, yellowish-white, granular nodules scattered across both the parietal and visceral peritoneal surfaces. This appearance is highly characteristic of **peritoneal carcinomatosis**, which occurs when a primary cancer (such as ovarian, gastric, or colorectal cancer) metastasizes and spreads throughout the peritoneal cavity. Other possibilities for this appearance could include miliary tuberculosis, although the overall presentation here strongly suggests malignancy.

A definitive diagnosis would require histopathological examination (biopsy) of the nodules under a microscope.
